messages.subject: STOP ERROR #6 in bears_optim_run() + NaNs produced in likelihood calculation
messages.subject_clean: STOP ERROR #6 in bears_optim_run() + NaNs produced in likelihood calculation
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have used BioGeoBEARS for multiple phylogenies in the last two years.
For this particular phylogeny, after running this code, I got the following error:

CODE for DEC model:

if (runslow)
{
  res = bears_optim_run(BioGeoBEARS_run_object)
  res

  save(res, file=resfn)
  resDEC = res
} else {
  load(resfn)
  resDEC = res
}

ERROR:

Error in bears_optim_run(BioGeoBEARS_run_object) :
  STOP ERROR #6 in bears_optim_run(). Test calculation of the likelihood with calc_loglike_for_optim() returned LnL=-1e+50, which is not a valid starting likelihood. Probably, you have an overly constrained analysis and have thus made your data impossible. For example, if your tips had ranges A and B, but you disallowed the state AB, then your data would be impossible under DEC, because AB is a required intermediate state. Try removing some of the areas allowed/area adjacency/manual states list constraints.  You can also try changing manual dispersal multipliers from 0 to some small value (e.g. 0.00001) -- note that this can works on dispersal multiplers, but NOT on area constraints, which have to be 0 or 1.  Have a CAREFUL THINK about what you are doing and why you think the list of ranges should be so constrained - do you actually have a good argument for your constraints?
In addition: Warning message:
In calc_loglike_sp(tip_condlikes_of_data_on_each_state = tip_condlikes_of_data_on_each_state,  :

Warning on error in dense exponentiation downpass (left branch): NaNs produced in likelihood calculation. This may mean your transition matrix disallows necessary transitions.  E.g., if your ranges are 'A' and 'B', and your model is DEC, then allowing range 'AB' as a possible state is required, so that you can get from 'A' to 'B' via 'AB' as the intermediate. Alternatively, NaNs can be produced sometimes if your Maximum Likelihood (ML) search proposes weird parameter values (such as a negative rate or weight) or a parameter so small that required transitions have a probability that machine precision rounds to zero or negative.  Sometimes this seems to occur because optim, optimx, etc. propose parameters slightly outside the user-specified upper and lower (min/max) boundaries for some reason. One solution is often to narrow the min/max limits.

You are using another solution: Normally, this would be a stop error, but you specified that BioGeoBEARS_run_object$on_NaN_error=-1e+50

DATA:

My geofile looks like this:
6 2 (X Y)
a 01
b 01
c 01
d 10
e 01
f 10

My newick file:

moref(trfn)
Read 1 item

((f:0.037678,e:0.037678):0.101711,(d:0.114221,(c:0.087662,(b:0.005593,a:0.005593):0.082069):0.02656):0.025167);

I also tried reducing the min. branch length to this: BioGeoBEARS_run_object$min_branchlength = 0.000000000001

Don't know what can be further modified. Hoping to get some help here.

Kind regards,
Bela

Ah, I see what it is. Change label.offset=0.45 to label.offset=0.0 throughout the script.  0.45 is normally a decent choice, but your whole phylogeny only covers 0.14 time units.

Since we're talking about your tree, things to consider if this is a real dataset (maybe this is just a small dataset to replicate a problem):

* Are these real time branchlengths?  Most phylogenies would cover more than 0.14 million years
* 6 tips in the tree is a very small dataset, essentially this is 6 data points, and each base model has 2 or 3 free parameters.  Normally you want at least 5-10 data points per free parameter you are estimating, and more if you are estimating a bunch of models. If that's not possible, at least the issue should be mentioned prominently in a paper's discussion of caveats.

Cheers,
Nick

For example, if your tips had ranges A and B, but you disallowed the state AB, then your data would be impossible under DEC, because AB is a required intermediate state. messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I think those saved results in "Table 2" are very old, from the first generation of the example script in 2013 or so. Since then the packages used for Maximum Likelihood inference (optim, optimx, GenSA) have been updated, defaults may have changed, etc. And, I must have changed the default minimum limit of parameters "d", "e", etc. from 1e-12 to 1e-7.

All of these things could cause small differences in the ML results, although as you can see they are very close. For BAYAREALIKE, the worst-fitting model, you see a little variation in the ML estimate of d, this probably suggests the likelihood surface is very flat under that model (remember, the ML optimizers work by "climbing the hill" of the likelihood surface -- they use heuristics that are pretty good but not always perfect). It doesn't matter very much, though, because BAYAREALIKE has hundreds of times worst fit than the other models.

Cheers!
Nick
